1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, King's Knight Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4.background: The same position arises from 1.c4 Nf6 2.Nf3. The English Opening is named after Howard Staunton, who played 1.c4 in his 1843 match against Saint-Amant and at London 1851, the first international tournament, but it caught on only in the twentieth century.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4.strategy: Fights for d5 from the flank without occupying the centre, and keeps both a central break with d4 and a kingside fianchetto available. White waits to see how Black sets up, and many different structures can arise by transposition. The cost is that no pawn stands in the centre yet, so Black chooses how to meet it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3.background: A common start of the King's Indian Attack, which Bobby Fischer (mostly in his early career), Mikhail Botvinnik, Vasily Smyslov and Tigran Petrosian all employed. Its use at grandmaster level began in the 1950s as an offshoot of the widespread King's Indian Defence, with White adopting Black's set-up with an extra move.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop on g2, where it bears on e4 and d5 along the long diagonal, and keeps White's central plans open. White castles early and builds from a safe king, which usually means a closed, strategic game. The cost is that the centre is left to Black, who can occupy it at once with ...d5.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.d4.strategy: Occupies the centre with a pawn and turns the game into a queen's pawn opening with the knight already on f3. White takes space and opens the c1-bishop, and Black must decide between contesting the centre at once and setting up from a distance. The early knight rules out set-ups that need the f-pawn on f3.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3.background: Named after Aron Nimzowitsch, who experimented with 1.b3 in the 1920s and 1930s and more often used the order 1.Nf3 d5 2.b3, and Bent Larsen, who played 1.b3 frequently from 1968 to 1972.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, which aims along the long diagonal at e5 and the knight on f6, and keeps the central pawns flexible. White lets Black take the centre and plans to undermine it later, in the manner of a flank opening. The cost is a slower claim on the centre, so Black can develop comfortably.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.e3.name: Zukertort Opening: Quiet System
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and supports a later d4. It is solid but slow, and once d4 follows, the e3-pawn shuts in the c1-bishop while Black is free to take space in the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.d3.strategy: Supports e4 and opens the c1-bishop, but it claims no space. It is sound but modest, and White's game stays passive until e4 can be played.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c3.strategy: Supports a later d4 and opens the d1–a4 diagonal for the queen, but it develops nothing and takes c3 from the queen's knight. It puts no pressure on Black's set-up, which can develop freely.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the second knight and watches e4 and d5 without committing a pawn. It blocks the c-pawn, so English set-ups with c4 are off for now, and Black takes the centre at once and can gain more space by chasing the knight.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a3.strategy: Prepares b4 and keeps a black bishop off b4, but does nothing for the centre or development. White is still waiting while Black takes space.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4.strategy: Gains queenside space on the rim, but spends a tempo on a pawn move that does nothing for the centre or development.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4.strategy: Advances the b-pawn where nothing defends it: after 2...e6 the f8-bishop attacks it, and White must spend another tempo on saving it or give it up to ...Bxb4. The advance also weakens c3 and leaves the queenside thin.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from a black knight or bishop, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn the position does not yet call for while White still has to develop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.h4.strategy: Gains kingside space and prepares h5, but loosens the kingside for no concrete gain and does nothing for the centre or development.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Rg1.strategy: Supports a later g4 and g5, but gives up the right to castle kingside and puts the rook on a closed file, so White's king stays in the middle.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Na3.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes b5 and c4 but guards nothing in the centre and blocks the a-pawn. Black's ...d5 also covers c4, and the knight stays out of play.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Ng5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to attack h7 and f7, both of which are defended. After 2...h6 it has to go back to f3 or h3, and Black gains time to take the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nh4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time, to the rim, where it watches f5 and g6 but does nothing for the centre. The knight is out of play while Black develops.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Ne5.strategy: Centralises the knight too early: 2...d6 attacks it and it must retreat, so White spends two moves for nothing while Black gains central space and opens the c8-bishop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nd4.strategy: Centralises the knight, but ...e5 or ...c5 attacks it at once and it must retreat, while Black gains central space with a tempo.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Ng1.strategy: Returns the knight to its starting square and undoes the first move, giving Black a free tempo with the knight already on f6. Black takes the centre at once while White has to start over.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.e4.strategy: Leaves the e4-pawn undefended, so 2...Nxe4 wins it. White's lead in development is doubtful compensation, and Black keeps an extra pawn in a sound position.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g4.strategy: Hangs a pawn: nothing defends g4, since the knight on f3 blocks the queen's diagonal, so 2...Nxg4 wins it. White's rook can then hit the knight, but it simply retreats and Black keeps the extra pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop's diagonal and prepares ...d5, keeping every set-up open: Black can still choose between a classical centre and a set-up with a fianchettoed bishop. The cost is the c8-bishop, which the e6-pawn shuts in until ...b6 gives it the long diagonal.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and quick castling, and leaves open whether Black strikes in the centre at once or builds up slowly. The cost is the centre: Black lets White occupy it first and relies on undermining it later with pawn breaks.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5.background: The same position arises from 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6. The Hedgehog Defence, a line of it, continues 3.g3 b6 4.Bg2 Bb7 5.Nc3 e6 6.O-O Be7 7.d4 cxd4 8.Qxd4 d6; the ideas behind the Hedgehog were originally developed in the English Opening, and it first became extensively analysed in the 1970s.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5.strategy: Controls d4, just as White's c-pawn controls d5, so White cannot take the centre for free. The cost is space: if White gets e4 in beside c4, Black's position is cramped and needs freeing breaks such as ...d5. The game is usually a manoeuvring fight over d4 and d5.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 b6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Queen's Indian Formation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 b6.background: The Queen's Indian Defence, a solid defence to the Queen's Pawn Game, takes its name from the fianchetto of Black's queen's bishop and is regarded as the sister opening of the Nimzo-Indian.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which adds to the f6-knight's control of e4 and d5 and claims the long diagonal. Black puts no pawn in the centre yet and controls it from a distance, which leaves White the choice of structure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Scandinavian Defence
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Challenges c4 at once. If White takes on d5, Black's knight has moved twice while White builds a centre with pawns. It is sound, but White chooses the structure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a Slav-type pawn chain that keeps the c8-bishop's diagonal open to develop outside the pawns. It is sound but passive, and the b8-knight loses c6 and usually develops via d7.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Old Indian Formation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d6.background: Siegbert Tarrasch introduced the Old Indian Defence in 1902, but it is more commonly associated with Mikhail Chigorin, who adopted it five years later and pioneered it late in his career. It is considered sound but has never attained the popularity of the King's Indian.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal, a modest set-up that can still turn into a fianchetto of the king's bishop. It is sound, but White can build a broad centre, and if the f8-bishop ends up on e7 rather than g7 Black is usually cramped.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps a central pawn advance in reserve, but the knight on c6 blocks the c-pawn and rules out ...c5 and ...c6. It is sound but less flexible than the main moves.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Puts the second knight on the rim, heading for b4 or c5, where it does nothing for the centre. White builds the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 against the c4-pawn but spends a tempo on a rook's pawn instead of developing a second piece. White builds the centre at leisure, and once the knight is on c3 the push ...b5 costs a pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 a5.strategy: Restrains b4 but spends a tempo on a rim pawn, weakens b5 and fights neither for the centre nor for development. White continues at leisure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn for queenside pressure, but without a White pawn on d5 and without ...c5 to open the queenside. After 3.cxb5 White keeps the extra pawn, and the pressure on the queenside does not make up for it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's pieces but spends a tempo on a rim pawn without developing anything or touching the centre. White continues undisturbed.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 h5.strategy: Supports a knight on g4 and prepares ...h4, but develops nothing and gives up ...h6 as a way to cover g5. White uses the free tempo to develop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Ng8.strategy: Returns the knight to g8 and undoes Black's only developing move. With c4 and Nf3 already played, White is two tempi ahead and can take the centre as it likes.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Ng4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time without a real threat, since the king guards f2 and the rook guards h2. After 3.h3 it has to retreat, and Black has lost time that White uses for the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Nh5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to the rim, where it no longer covers d5 or e4. White builds the centre while the knight on h5 takes no part in the fight for it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Ne4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to e4, where no pawn supports it. 3.d3 drives it away at once, and White gains time for the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Rg8.strategy: Gives up kingside castling for good and develops nothing, since the rook has no work on g8. White builds the centre while Black's king can at best castle long.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 e5.strategy: Leaves the pawn en prise: 3.Nxe5 wins it, and Black has no real compensation, since White keeps the pawn and simply develops.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn, which the f3-knight attacks and nothing defends, since the e7-pawn blocks the queen's diagonal. After 3.Nxg5 White is a pawn up and Black's kingside is loosened for nothing.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 Nd5.strategy: Hangs the knight: 3.cxd5 wins it outright, since the d7-pawn blocks the queen from recapturing and nothing else covers d5.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5.name: King's Indian Attack
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5.background: Relatively uncommon at grandmaster level today, with Bassem Amin its most frequent high-level practitioner, but popular at club level for its repeatable middlegame plans. The trainer Mark Dvoretsky advocated the system and played it himself.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and keeps the c8-bishop free to develop outside the pawn chain. The cost is a committed d-pawn, which gives White a clear target for c4 and the plan of building up with d3 and e4. The game tends to be closed and strategic, with White setting the pace.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's kingside fianchetto: the bishop will watch the long diagonal and the king can castle early, while the centre stays open for later. If White takes space with c4 and d4, the game becomes a King's Indian or a Grünfeld with White's bishop on g2. The cost is a slower claim on the centre than ...d5 makes at once.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 c5.strategy: Controls d4, so White cannot easily build a broad centre, and keeps the d-pawn flexible. Black can head for a symmetrical set-up or for a Reversed King's Indian, taking White's usual role. The c-pawn occupies no central square yet, so both sides keep their options.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 with a solid set-up. The cost is the c8-bishop, which stays shut in behind the e6-pawn unless Black finds a way out, such as a queenside fianchetto; White's slow build-up with d3 and e4 aims at exactly that. White can also take space with c4 and d4, with the g2-bishop pressing on the long diagonal.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 b5.name: King's Indian Attack: Spassky Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 b5.background: Sometimes called the Spassky Variation after Boris Spassky's use of ...b5 against Tigran Petrosian in the 1966 World Championship match, although that game, the decisive 22nd, began 1.d4 b5. The line is fully respectable and has been played successfully by grandmasters including former world champions Mikhail Tal, Anatoly Karpov and Magnus Carlsen.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 b5.strategy: Gains queenside space and prepares ...Bb7 to contest the long diagonal. Unlike ...b6, it discourages c4, since the pawn on b5 could take there. The price is a pawn that can become a target for White's a-pawn and knight and a loosened queenside.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to oppose the bishop on g2 on the long diagonal. The set-up is sound, but unlike ...b5 it does not discourage c4, so White can take space in the centre or play quietly.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight towards d4 and e5 and prepares ...e5, which it would support. It blocks the c-pawn, ruling out ...c5 for now, and White can take the centre with d4. The move is sound but less flexible than set-ups that keep the c-pawn free.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn chain, with the c8-bishop free to go to f5 or g4 once the d-pawn advances. The move does nothing for the centre yet, so White can take the centre first. Sound, but ...d5 at once reaches the same set-ups and keeps the c-pawn free for ...c5.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and a compact set-up behind it. It opens the c8-bishop but concedes central space, so White can build a broad centre. Sound, though passive.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 a6.strategy: A slow move that prepares ...b5, which Black can play at once, so it simply loses a tempo while White builds the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 a5.strategy: Gains space on the queenside and controls b4, but does nothing for development or the centre, so White can build up undisturbed.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Develops the knight to the edge, where it eyes b4 and c5 but has little influence on the centre. White gains time to build there.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Rg8.strategy: Spends a tempo and gives up kingside castling for good, since the h8-rook has moved, without helping development or the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Ng8.strategy: Undoes the first move. Black has spent two tempi to return to the start while White has developed the knight and prepared the fianchetto, with a free hand in the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 h6.strategy: A prophylactic pawn move that spends a tempo with nothing yet to prevent. It does not help development or the centre, so White can build up at leisure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 h5.strategy: Heads for ...h4 to attack the g3-pawn, but weakens g5 and loosens the kingside before Black has developed. It does nothing for the centre, so White builds it undisturbed.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Ng4.strategy: The knight eyes f2 and h2 from g4, but 3.h3 chases it at once, and 3...Ne5 then loses it to Nxe5. After the retreat to f6 or h6 Black has lost two tempi and White has played h3 for free.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Nh5.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes g3 and f4 but contests no central square. White can build the centre, or drive it away at once with 3.g4, gaining kingside space with tempo.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Nd5.strategy: Centralises the knight, but 3.c4 attacks it at once and it must retreat, for example to b6. White gains time for a broad centre, while Black has spent three moves on one knight.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Ne4.strategy: Eyes f2 and g3, but 3.d3 attacks the knight at once and it must retreat to f6, d6 or c5, losing time while White gains d3 for free. Capturing on g3 only gives a knight for a pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g5.strategy: Hangs a pawn: the knight on f6 does not guard g5, so 3.Nxg5 simply wins it, and Black's kingside is left loose.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 e5.strategy: Hangs the e-pawn: nothing defends e5, so 3.Nxe5 simply wins it. After 3...Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6 Black's queen and c8-bishop have open lines, but Black is a clean pawn down.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and, together with the f6-knight, makes it hard for White to achieve e4. The b2-bishop will bite on a solid pawn centre that White has to undermine, while Black develops in a straightforward way. The cost is some flexibility, since the d-pawn is committed early.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 g6.strategy: Answers White's fianchetto with one of its own: the g7-bishop will challenge the b2-bishop on the long diagonal. The set-up is flexible and keeps ...c5 available, but until Black castles the g7-bishop is undefended, so a careless move of the f6-knight can drop it to Bxg7.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 e6.strategy: Opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and keeps the choice of set-up open, from a classical centre to a Queen's Indian style fianchetto. The price is a c8-bishop that stays shut in behind the e6-pawn until Black frees it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 c5.strategy: Contests d4 at once, answering White's flank play with a strike at the centre, and keeps the pawn set-up flexible. The game tends towards symmetrical English-style structures, quiet and manoeuvring, where neither side commits early.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 b6.strategy: Copies White's set-up: the c8-bishop will meet the b2-bishop on the long diagonal, in Queen's Indian style. The structure is solid but somewhat passive, since Black has little quick counterplay and mostly reacts to White's plan.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and eyes d4 and e5, but the knight blocks the c-pawn and commits itself before Black's structure is clear. Once Bb2 is played, ...e5 would leave the pawn attacked twice and defended once, so Black has to prepare it first.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d6.strategy: Prepares to take space in the centre or to fianchetto the king's bishop. The move is modest: it does not contest e4 as ...d5 does, and White develops freely.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a Slav-style pawn pair and keeps the c8-bishop free. It is solid but slower than ...d5 at once and takes c6 away from the b8-knight, so White gets time to develop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn that neither fights for the centre nor develops a piece. White takes the lead in development.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 a5.strategy: Prepares ...a4 against the b3-pawn, but spends a tempo on the flank while the centre is uncontested, and the a-pawn can no longer cover b6 or b5. White develops undisturbed.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 b5.strategy: Weakens the queenside: after e3 the f1-bishop attacks b5, so …a6 or …c6 is needed to hold the pawn, and Black's development falls behind.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move although nothing needs to be prevented on g5, and the centre stays uncontested. White develops undisturbed.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 h5.strategy: Pushes the rook pawn without a purpose and loses a tempo while the centre stays uncontested. White simply goes on developing.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, aiming at b4 or c5, without doing anything for the centre. Once e3 opens the f1-bishop's diagonal, Bxa6 bxa6 would double Black's a-pawns.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Ng8.strategy: Retreats the only developed piece to its starting square and undoes the single useful move Black has made. White gains two tempi and develops at leisure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Ng4.strategy: Sends the knight to a square where h3 chases it away at once; …Ne5 hangs to Nxe5, so it has to retreat to f6 or h6, and White has gained a tempo with h3.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Nh5.strategy: Places the knight on the rim to reach f4, but g3 takes that square away and leaves f6 as its only safe square, while the move does nothing for the centre or for development.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Ne4.strategy: Centralises the knight too early: d3 kicks it at once and White gains a free move, since the retreat to c5 runs into b4 and the one to d6 blocks the d-pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Nd5.strategy: Puts the knight on a square where e4 or c4 hits it with tempo; White then builds a broad pawn centre, while Black's knight has spent three moves and been driven back.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 e5.strategy: Hangs the e-pawn: 3.Nxe5 wins it because nothing recaptures on e5, and 3…Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6 only trades pieces without regaining the pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 g5.strategy: Loses a pawn to 3.Nxg5: the e7-pawn and the f6-knight block the queen's diagonal, so nothing defends g5, and the advance also weakens the kingside.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 Rg8.strategy: Forfeits kingside castling and sends the rook to a closed file, achieving nothing in the centre or in development. White simply goes on developing while Black's king has lost its natural home.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 g6.strategy: Ignores White's flank pawn move and prepares the kingside fianchetto, so the bishop on g7 will bear on the long diagonal. The advance of the a-pawn has done nothing for White's centre or development, so Black can develop at ease and keep every set-up open.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 g6.strategy: Meets the flank advance with a plain fianchetto: the bishop on g7 will bear on the long diagonal that White's b-pawn has just left open. Black develops sensibly and lets White's early pawn advance prove itself, since the b4 pawn has no pawn support.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Mirrors White's development and aims at the centre: the knight eyes d4 and e5 while Black keeps all pawn set-ups open. Quiet and flexible, it asks White to declare a plan, since neither side has yet committed to a structure.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.Nc3 Nc6.name: Zukertort Opening

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 g6 3.b4.name: Zukertort Opening: Myers Polish Attack
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.a4 g6 3.b4.strategy: Adds a second flank pawn advance before the centre or the pieces are looked after. It grabs queenside space and prepares a bishop on b2, but the pawns on a4 and b4 can only be defended by pieces, and the long diagonal stands open for Black's fianchettoed bishop until White's own bishop arrives.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2.strategy: Completes the queenside fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal at f6 and the kingside, while the b3 pawn covers c4. White lets Black hold a pawn in the centre and plans to undermine it from a distance rather than occupy it, keeping the choice of pawn break for later.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 straight away, claiming queenside space and making a central advance hard for White. Black builds a pawn centre on d5 and c5 that White will try to undermine with piece pressure, so the game turns on whether that centre proves a strength or a target.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up: the fianchettoed bishop will oppose the bishop on b2 along the long diagonal, while the d5 pawn holds the centre. Black chooses a solid, evenly balanced game over grabbing queenside space and keeps the c-pawn flexible.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 c5 4.e4.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Norfolk Gambit
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 c5 4.e4.strategy: A pawn offer in the centre: both ...dxe4 and ...Nxe4 win it, because nothing defends it. White hopes that the bishop's diagonal, which opens towards g7 if the f6-knight takes, and quick play against Black's centre will pay for it, but White has to justify the pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6 4.c4.strategy: Challenges the d5 pawn at once, so Black has to resolve the central tension instead of simply developing. White fights for the centre with a wing pawn and a long-diagonal bishop rather than a pawn centre, and puts the c-pawn to work for queenside space.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6 4.c4 c6.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, Bled Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2 g6 4.c4 c6.strategy: Defends d5 with a pawn, so a capture on d5 is met by ...cxd5 and Black keeps a pawn in the centre. It builds a solid wall of pawns behind which the g7-bishop will bear on the long diagonal against White's bishop, and keeps Black's structure free of weaknesses.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 g6 3.Bb2.name: Sokolsky Opening: Zukertort System
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.b4 g6 3.Bb2.strategy: Brings the bishop onto the long diagonal at once, where it faces Black's coming fianchetto and presses on f6. The b4 pawn gains queenside space but has no pawn behind it, so White commits to a flank game: a fianchetto duel in which White hopes to profit from the extra space on the wing.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to the square that watches d5 and e4, so Black's own central advance is hard to achieve. White keeps the central advance in reserve and plays for a lasting, slight initiative in a mirror-image pawn structure where both sides hold the same flank pawns.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.b4.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Napolitano Gambit
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.b4.strategy: Offers a flank pawn at once, hoping to deflect Black's c-pawn from the centre and win queenside activity. Black simply takes it with ...cxb4 and is a pawn up, and White's compensation is thin, since only the f3-knight is developed to make use of the open lines.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3.strategy: Supports the c4 pawn and prepares the bishop on the long diagonal. White leaves the d-pawn at home, preferring to see how Black declares the centre and then to fight for d5 with pieces from a distance, in the manner of a flexible flank opening.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once with a pawn that c6 already supports, and hits the c4 pawn. White's b3 holds it, so the tension is stable, and Black gets a solid structure and a clear claim to the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop eyes the long diagonal and the kingside, while the b3 pawn keeps c4 defended against the d5 pawn. White chooses piece pressure and flexibility over an immediate central advance, and awaits Black's plan for the light-squared bishop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, New York System
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain while it still can, before ...e6 shuts it in, and eyes the b1-knight and the d3 square. Black gets an active piece for free and keeps a solid centre; the bishop may have to retreat later if White challenges it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, Capablanca Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4.strategy: Puts pressure on the f3-knight, which only the e- and g-pawns defend, and threatens to trade it and take away its control of e5 and d4. Black also gets the bishop out before ...e6, at the price of spending a move that White's pieces can try to use.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5 5.e3.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, New York System
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5 5.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop's diagonal and prepares quick castling in a solid set-up. White lets Black's bishop keep its active diagonal for now and decides the central plan later, preferring sound development to an early attempt to harass the bishop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5 5.d3.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, New York System
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bf5 5.d3.strategy: Cuts the f5-bishop's view of the b1-knight at d3 and covers e4, but the pawn on d3 also shuts the f1-bishop's diagonal, which has to come out by another route. A modest move that slows White's own development to reduce Black's activity.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4 5.e3.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, Capablanca Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4 5.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop's diagonal and prepares quick development. If Black trades on f3, the queen recaptures without damaging White's pawns. A solid, flexible answer that keeps the centre in reserve and leaves it to Black to decide whether to trade the bishop.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4 5.d3.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, Capablanca Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 c6 3.b3 d5 4.Bb2 Bg4 5.d3.strategy: Keeps the e-pawn flexible and supports a later central advance, but the pawn on d3 shuts the f1-bishop's diagonal, so that piece can come out only to e2 or after a kingside fianchetto. A modest set-up that develops more slowly than the alternative.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn to clear the centre: the c-pawn is traded for Black's d-pawn, leaving White with d- and e-pawns against Black's single e-pawn in the middle. The game then turns on whether that central majority outweighs the activity Black's pieces gain.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence, Scandinavian Defence, Exchange Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 d5 3.cxd5 Nxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, which lands on the best central square and keeps the queen at home. Black has traded the d-pawn for White's c-pawn and plays for piece activity against White's central pawn majority, but must take care not to lose time when the knight is challenged.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2.strategy: Develops the bishop to its post on the long diagonal and prepares castling. White has a flexible set-up: the centre can be taken with the e-pawn or with the c-pawn, and Black must decide how to meet a system rather than a particular move.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 c6.strategy: Supports the d5 pawn while leaving the queen's bishop free to develop outside the pawn chain. A solid, compact set-up that avoids the cramped bishop that the other natural defence brings.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6.name: King's Indian Attack, with e6
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the way for the king's bishop. It is solid, but the queen's bishop is shut in behind the e6 and d5 pawns, so Black must find a plan to bring it into play while White builds up patiently.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O.strategy: Castles before committing the centre. White's set-up is complete and the choice of central plan stays open, which is the strength of the system: Black has to guess which pawn break is coming.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O Be7.name: King's Indian Attack, with e6
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O Be7.strategy: Brings the king's bishop out and prepares to castle, keeping the position compact and safe. Black is solid but still waiting: White has finished development and can pick the plan that suits it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O Be7 5.c.strategy: Gives up the slower plan with the e-pawn and presses on the d5 pawn directly. The position takes on the character of a closed game in which White's pieces and the c-pawn together test Black's centre.
